intro_slide_description1: Visible light is the rays of 390 nm and 780 nm wavelength, which occupies a very small place in the light spectrum. Blue light is the radiations of wavelengths between 390 nm and 470 nm. Color temperatures above 5000 K are cool colors ie bluish Lower color temperatures (2700-3000 K) are called "warm colors" (yellowish colors). As the wavelength of the light decreases, the color of the light starts to turn blue / purple and the Kelvin (K) value increases.
intro_slide_title2: What is the color temperature, Kelvin (K)?
intro_slide_description2: The color temperature is a measure of the color of the light and is expressed in Kelvin (K). The light emitted from the screen with a high Kelvin value (above 5000 K) emits" blue light ". Blue light causes some damage to your eyes and body. It happens.
intro_slide_description3: In order to sleep, the human body releases the hormone melatonin. The insufficiency of the hormone melatonin at night will cause your sleep to come off. For the melatonin to be secreted, the environment should be dark and you should not be exposed to blue light. In the daytime, your body, which receives sunlight, stops the release of the hormone melatonin. When the blue wavelength decreases and the sun starts to set, your body slowly starts to increase the level of melatonin hormone, that is, it enters the night mode. Exposure to blue light at night gives our body a message that " the sun is still not set now, entering the night mode." You have difficulty falling asleep :(

about_what_body: DoctorFilter lays a warm, dimmable tint over your screen. In the evening this lowers the amount of short-wavelength light reaching your eyes, which is the light your body reads as daytime.
about_science_title: How the numbers are worked out
about_science_body: Colour temperatures are converted using the Planckian locus in CIE 1931 and turned back into Kelvin by finding the nearest point on that curve, so the number on screen is the colour actually being drawn. The reduction figure is melanopic, following CIE S 026, and comes straight from the filter's own maths rather than being estimated.
about_disclaimer_body: DoctorFilter is not a medical device. It does not diagnose, treat or prevent any condition, and it is not a substitute for advice from an eye-care professional. If your eyes hurt, water, or your vision changes, see a doctor.

edu_spectrum_title: Visible light and your body clock
edu_spectrum_body: Visible light runs from about 380 to 780 nm. Alongside the cells you see with, your eyes carry receptors containing melanopsin that are most sensitive around 480 nm. They do not contribute much to vision — they tell your brain what time of day it is.
edu_kelvin_body: Kelvin describes the colour of a light source by comparing it to a heated object. A candle flame sits near 1850 K, a warm bulb near 2700 K, and midday daylight above 5500 K. The lower the number, the less short-wavelength light.
edu_melanopic_body: Researchers measure evening light as melanopic EDI. A 2022 expert consensus recommends staying under 10 lx melanopic EDI in the three hours before bed, and under 1 lx while asleep. DoctorFilter shows how far its current settings move you in that direction.
edu_dimming_body: A 2019 study of Apple's Night Shift found that changing a screen's colour without lowering its brightness did not meaningfully reduce melatonin suppression. Warm colours help, but the extra dim slider is doing more of the work.
edu_strain_body: Screen fatigue is mostly caused by blinking less, focusing up close for hours and dry air — not by blue light. A 2023 Cochrane review of 17 trials found blue-light filtering lenses probably make no difference to eye strain. The reliable advice is the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Blink deliberately.
edu_sources_note: Brown et al., PLOS Biology 2022 · Nagare et al., 2019 · Singh et al., Cochrane 2023 · CIE S 026:2018
